doc.title: Håkan Rydin interviewed by Monk Rowe, Glasgow, Scotland, July 27, 2016

chapter: Playing with Fame and Kim Parker
title: Kim Parker, her mother Chan Parker and Charlie Parker's painting and estate
summary: Fifteen years accompanying Kim Parker; visit to Chan Parker's home, Bird's painting, and the family's income from the film and the plastic sax.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: And you spent some years accompanying Kim Parker?

Yes I did. We played I think almost 15 years off and on. Of course not all the time but off and on. And I still have contact with her. I also got to know her fantastic mother, Chan Parker, the wife of Bird. So for example we went to her home, she lived outside Paris, in a 200 year old house or something, and at the bottom floor it was just one big room. It had a kitchen where you eat, you had the living room, and you had the music department. So it was like that. And on the walls there was “Best Alto Saxophone Player ’47, ’48, ’49.” The Down Beat award. For Bird. And there was a big painting that Bird did. Maybe you know, he was also a great painter, painting in oil. And it was a painting he did in the late 40s, a big painting. It looks exactly like Kim Parker when she is 25 or 30. It’s amazing. You can’t explain it. It’s like a portrait. But he did it when Kim was two years old.
I wonder if Chan was able to live off any of Charlie Parker’s estate, or if there was such a thing.

To some extent but they very seldom got anything from the record companies, because Bird didn’t have that kind of agreement. He had a cash payment. No contracts. They got a lot of money from Clint Eastwood when they made the film. Clint was very nice to the family, inviting them for the premier and talking to them in the production, so he did good and the family had the two saxes, saxophones, so first they sold the plastic —
The plastic sax. They got a lot of money for that. The other one I won’t talk about. But they said it was like their insurance.
